Threat.value: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger

Negative Appraisals.value: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper
I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me
The world is a dangerous place

issues.item: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: For a man-made disaster trauma in a 58-year-old forensic analyst, this item is only coherent if there was a significant physical injury. The rest of the selected profile does not support an injury-based presentation: the threat items emphasize environmental danger and vigilance (limited safe places, loud sounds, unfamiliar places), while the other appraisals are about coping failure and loss of capability rather than concrete bodily injury. With no memory or strategy items to anchor a physical-injury narrative, this appraisal stands out as clinically hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
issues.explanation: The profile is not coherent with the supplied cognitive formulation because all cross-node edges are inactive, which implies these components should not appear as tightly linked aspects of one maintaining pattern. However, the Threat items and Negative Appraisal items are strongly conceptually connected: perceiving the world as dangerous maps directly onto restricted safety zones and avoidance of unfamiliar places, creating an active Threat–Negative Appraisal linkage that contradicts the formulation.

issues.item: Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
issues.explanation: Within the selected nodes, the content clusters into a classic mutually reinforcing danger/coping pattern rather than isolated components. 'World is a dangerous place' coheres directly with hypervigilance to sounds and avoidance of unfamiliar places, while 'Bad Coper' and 'No longer capable' reflect generalized post-trauma self-evaluation likely tied to the same threat response. With no active edges anywhere in the formulation, this degree of integration is inconsistent.

issues.item: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
issues.explanation: The formulation specifies no active edges, so the selected nodes should function as relatively isolated components rather than implying a tight linked syndrome. Here the Threat items and Negative Appraisal items form a classic connected PTSD pattern: danger-focused hypervigilance/startle and avoidance are closely mirrored by broad beliefs that the world is dangerous and that the self is incapable. This actively implies strong Threat↔Negative Appraisal linkage, which contradicts the fully disconnected formulation.

issues.item: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
issues.explanation: Within Threat, the items are coherent with each other, and within Negative Appraisals the items are also coherent. The problem is cross-node/formulation consistency: the profile presents mutually reinforcing danger sensitivity and negative self/world beliefs despite all edges being inactive.

vignette: Fifteen years ago, Mateo was walking through the lower level of a chemical processing facility when an overloaded transformer ruptured. The initial spark triggered a chain reaction, and within minutes, thick smoke poured from the ventilation shafts while the automated fire doors began to lower. He remembered the sudden loss of familiar landmarks, the way the emergency lighting cast long, distorted shadows, and the panic of realizing the main corridor he had just traversed was already sealing off. He spent the next twenty minutes pressing his ear against unfamiliar concrete walls, tapping blindly for hollow space, and calculating which stairwell might still be open. When he finally squeezed through a partially ajar service door into the cool evening air, his chest was tight, his vision narrowed, and his hands would not stop trembling. In the years that followed, Mateo built a career as a Forensic Analyst, a role that demanded precision and a steady hand. Yet the laboratory environment itself became the ground where his fears took root. During a routine walkthrough of the evidence processing wing, he found himself standing at the intersection of the archival corridor and the newly installed intake bay. The layout did not align with the building’s original blueprint. He could not assess the danger. He traced the sightlines to the nearest marked exit, counted the available doorways, and when the configuration felt unanchored, he simply turned back. He could not bring himself to walk into a space where the escape routes were uncertain. His daily life settled into a quiet rhythm of parallel experiences. His body felt constantly tense and ready to react to danger, a posture that never fully relaxed even in the fluorescent-lit conference room. A dropped stapler in the breakroom made him flinch so sharply that he had to brace himself against the counter. When the overhead ventilation system kicked on with a sudden mechanical hum, his shoulders drew up and his breath shortened. He had come to believe that his constant physical readiness showed he was a lousy coper. Looking at his reflection in the lab’s glass filing cabinets, he was certain that he was no longer capable of doing the things that had defined him—moving through a room without scanning it, trusting his own pace, working without bracing for a collapse of order. The world, he thought, was a dangerous place, and certainty was the only shield he could trust. Over months and years, these reactions hardened into habits. He stopped volunteering for regional site assessments. He began arriving to the county facility ten minutes before his shift, sitting in his parked car until the parking garage felt sufficiently mapped. His wife, Elena, noticed how he would pause at the threshold of new restaurants, how he would leave the television off during summer thunderstorms, how he no longer joined her for weekend walks because he preferred to stay where the paths were known. The occupational consequences accumulated steadily; he was transitioned to a desk-bound review position, which brought administrative stability but also a quiet, persistent grief for the hands-on work he once loved. What finally brought Mateo to the clinic was a quarterly audit that required him to walk through an unmarked logistics corridor with a visiting inspector. Standing in the echoing concrete space, his muscles locked, his breathing shallow, he realized he could no longer navigate his own days by instinct. He wanted to stop bracing for the next moment of disorientation. He was hoping, quietly, to find a way to step into a room without immediately calculating whether he could make it out.
